A B S T R A C T
The rapid growth of 3D printing technology has led to an increase in polymeric waste, which requires proper 
management to avoid further pressure on the end-of-waste system. In this context, anaerobic digestion (AD) is a 
promising strategy for biorenewable energy production (e.g., biomethane) when biodegradable polymers, such 
as polylactic acid (PLA), are employed. Indeed, the latter has been widely used as a bioactive polymer for 3D 
printing, but the high printing temperatures can alter its properties, thereby affecting its biodegradability. This 
study investigated, for the first time, the biodegradation of 3D-printing PLA waste via AD under mesophilic 
conditions for 63 days. With the aim of improving the biodegradability of 3D-printing-derived waste, various 
process-based strategies, including micro-aeration, Fenton oxidation, and thermo-alkaline pretreatment, were 
thus employed. Biogas production and speciation during AD, as well as weight loss of PLA samples (i.e., un­
treated, unprinted, and printed), and their further characterization through differential scanning calorimetry 
analysis, FT-IR spectroscopy, and viscometrical measurements were assessed to study the effectiveness of the 
investigated process-based strategy. The combined thermo-alkaline pretreatment (i.e., 2.5 %w/v of Ca(OH)2 at 
70 ◦C for 72 h) applied on 3D-printed PLA samples resulted in a total weight loss of 83.1% after AD process and a 
biomethane yield of approximately 360 mL/gPLA, which were significantly higher than that achieved with the 
control samples (i.e., 30% and <100 mL/gPLA, respectively). These results provided practical insights for the 
integration of additive manufacturing waste into AD-based circular economy strategies.
1. Introduction
Three-dimensional (3D) printing is a manufacturing process used to 
make objects from a digital Computer-Aided Design (CAD) model 
through a layer-by-layer material deposition approach. Among the 
various additive manufacturing technologies developed in the last de­
cades, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is one of the most widely used 
open-source technologies, being FDM printers compact, affordable, and 
with low effort for minimal maintenance [1]. In general, during this 
process, a thermoplastic filament is heated above its melting point, 
extruded through a nozzle under controlled shear, and deposited in 
successive layers, where it quickly solidifies upon cooling to generate 
the final element. Although 3D printing was originally developed for 
rapid prototyping and modeling, it has evolved into a promising and 
widely adopted method for producing final, end-use products across 
multiple sectors, including consumer goods, biomedical devices, and 
engineering applications [2].
Despite the rapid development of FDM led to increased material 
throughput, it has also placed pressure on the waste management system 
due to a significant stream of polymeric waste. For instance, Song and

Telenko [3] reported that polymeric waste from FDM printing accounts 
for 34% of the plastic used. Similarly, it has been reported that at least 
5000 tons of waste were produced in 2020, over an annual consumption 
for 3D printing of 18,500 tons of plastic material [4].
Several approaches can be used to address the plastic waste issue 
management, including re-extrusion and the use of biodegradable 
plastics. About this, one of the main biodegradable plastics involved in 
3D printing is indeed represented by polylactic acid (PLA) [5]. The latter 
is more environmentally friendly than conventional polymers (e.g., 
polyethylene), but 3D printing can affect this beneficial feature. Indeed, 
PLA filaments undergo repeated thermal and mechanical stresses during 
the FDM process, which can induce chain scission, reduce molecular 
weight, and modify crystallization behavior [6,7]. Therefore, due to the 
loss of mechanical properties after many recycling cycles, manufacturers 
are discouraged from adopting this practice. In addition, the FDM pro­
cess could influence the biodegradability of FDM waste, casting doubt 
on the applicability of eco-friendly treatment approaches as alternatives 
to landfilling, such as biological processes.
Among biological processes, anaerobic digestion (AD) represents a 
suitable option to deal with biodegradable waste due to its effectiveness 
in decreasing the waste amount while producing biorenewable energy 
through biomethane production. Indeed, PLA is considered a biode­
gradable biopolymer according to international standards, such as EN 
13432, ASTM D6400, ISO 14853, and ISO 17088, which define the re­
quirements for aerobic/anaerobic biodegradation under controlled in­
dustrial composting/AD conditions [8]. For instance, it was observed 
that mesophilic AD carried out for over 75-90 days resulted in a 1-7% 
PLA degradation, while higher biodegradation (more than 80%) and 
biomethanation were achieved in about 2 months, but through ther­
mophilic conditions [9–14]. However, due to the changes in the 
physical-chemical properties of FDM waste (i.e., surface areas, molec­
ular weight, crystallinity, etc.) compared to the pristine materials [15], 
AD effectiveness can be altered.
Since thermophilic AD can be energetically unfeasible (i.e., negative 
energy balance) [16], the limited anaerobic conversion of PLA under 
mesophilic conditions represents a relevant technological challenge and 
one of the main motivations of the present study, which aimed at 
evaluating whether different process-based strategies could enhance the 
anaerobic digestion of 3D-printing-derived PLA waste and improve 
biogas production.
Therefore, to enhance the conversion of recalcitrant substrates, 
several process-based strategies, such as micro-aeration, Fenton oxida­
tion, and thermo-alkaline pretreatment, have been developed to 
improve hydrolysis and biodegradation. Micro-aeration [17,18], a 
controlled oxygen dosing, was applied during AD to stimulate hydrolytic 
and facultative microbial activity, enhance redox balance, and accel­
erate the breakdown of recalcitrant waste. Also, oxidative pretreatments 
(e.g., Fenton-like processes) generate reactive oxygen species that can 
induce surface oxidation and partial chain cleavage [19,20]. 
Thermo-alkaline pretreatments, including Ca(OH)2 addition at mild 
temperatures (e.g., 70 ◦C), can promote ester bond hydrolysis via 
nucleophilic attack, thereby reducing molecular weight and increasing 
solubility [21,22].
Although these approaches were mostly investigated for lignocellu­
losic materials (LMs), their potential impact on 3D-printed PLA waste, i. 
e., material already thermo-mechanically degraded [23,24], remains 
unexplored. For instance, a previous study reporting cold plasma 
treatment on PLA for food packaging also displayed an increase of the 
material hydrophilic nature and shorter molecular chains, both 
providing better conditions for microbial attachment on the treated PLA 
surface and fragmentation [25]. Also, previous studies only investigated 
the effect of other process-based strategies (i.e., PLA codigestion during 
AD) [26] or used pristine material in forms of pellets [27,28], sometimes 
mechanically reduced to powder [10,28,29], films [25,29], or pieces 
obtained from commercial items [30,31].
Therefore, to fill this knowledge gap, the present work focused on: (i) 
the investigation of AD for unprinted PLA (UnP-PLA) filament and 
printed PLA (P-PLA); (ii) the comparative evaluation of different 
process-based strategies (i.e., micro-aeration, Fenton-oxidation, and 
thermo-alkaline pretreatment) on the thermo-mechanically modified 
PLA; (iii) the mechanistic interpretation of the observed biodegradation 
behavior via integrated FT-IR, DSC, viscometry, weight-loss, and soluble 
chemical oxygen demand (COD) analyses; (iv) a kinetic evaluation based 
on the modified Gompertz model to investigate methane-production 
dynamics under the different process-based strategies and (v) the iden­
tification of the most effective strategy for enhancing biomethane pro­
duction from 3D-printed PLA after a preliminary techno-economic 
assessment.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
2.1.1. Polylactic acid and printing procedure
A white PLA Ingeo 850 filament, purchased from Eolas Prints 
(Spain), was used for this study. This is a highly crystalline PLA with a 
diameter of 1.75 mm, a density of 124 g/cm3, and a melting point of 165 
– 180 ◦C. The UnP-PLA filament used for the experiments was cut into 
3.8 cm-long rods weighing 0.109 ± 0.005 g. The P-PLA sticks were 
printed on a Delta WASP 2040 PRO 3D printer equipped with a SPIT­
FIRE extruder at 195 ◦C, with the print bed maintained at 50 ◦C. Spe­
cifically, the P-PLA was vertically printed on a 0.5 cm-thick base, with a 
resulting stick length of 4 cm and a diameter equal to that of the starting 
filament (1.75 mm) (Fig. 1). The obtained P-PLA sticks weighed 
0.109 ± 0.005 g, equal to that of the UnP-PLA filaments. Both UnP-PLA 
filaments and P-PLA sticks were stored in an airtight bag containing 
silica gel to maintain the polymer at low humidity.
2.1.2. Anaerobic inoculum
The anaerobic inoculum used for the AD tests was obtained from the 
first-stage mesophilic anaerobic digester of a full-scale wastewater 
treatment plant (WWTP) in Monopoli (Puglia, Italy). During sampling, 
the sludge was sieved to remove particles larger than 0.4 mm. To reduce 
residual biodegradable organic matter prior to the biochemical methane 
potential (BMP) assays and to accurately detect biogas produced solely 
from PLA biodegradation, the sludge was preliminarily incubated using 
a procedure adapted from Elbeshbishy et al. [32]. In brief, the 150 mL 
inoculum was placed in 0.25 L in PYREX glass bottles and pre-incubated 
at 35 ± 2 ◦C for 10 days under anaerobic conditions by flushing the 
headspace with argon gas. After pre-incubation, the inoculum showed a 
concentration of total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), soluble COD,

2.2. Experimental procedures
2.2.1. Anaerobic digestion of UnP-PLA and P-PLA
The AD of PLA samples was carried out in PYREX glass bottles 
(0.25 L), closed with airtight caps equipped with a biogas sampling pipe, 
under mesophilic (35 ± 2 ◦C) conditions for 63 d, i.e., until the cumu­
lative biogas production reached a plateau. The bottles were filled with 
150 mL of inoculum and 0.65 g PLA as described in Table 2. Each bottle 
was flushed with Ar to remove air from the headspace. Under these 
conditions, considering a COD input of 1.5 gCOD/gPLA [28], the feed on 
microorganism ratio (F/M) was equal to 0.62 gCODPLA/gVSinoculum, 
which can support high COD removal efficiencies [33]. Control tests 
(CTRL) were prepared under identical operating conditions, without 
PLA addition, to determine the contribution of PLA biodegradation to 
biogas production (mL). Each test was carried out in triplicate.
2.3. Process-based strategies for enhancing anaerobic biodegradation of 
PLA
2.3.1. Anaerobic digestion with micro-aeration approach
AD with micro-aeration (μAIR-AD) was also tested for 63 d on UnP- 
PLA and P-PLA. These tests were carried out in 2.5 L PYREX glass bottles, 
closed with airtight screw caps equipped with a biogas sampling pipe 
and a tube for the entry of air, under mesophilic (35 ± 2 ◦C) conditions. 
As described in Table 3, the reactors were filled with 1 L of inoculum, 
4.16 g PLA, and 19 mL/d of air [34]. The air was insufflated throughout 
the whole experiment into the bottom of the reactors with a syringe 
pump to respect the optimal oxygen supply of 0.38 mL O2/g VS/d [35]. 
Before the beginning of the AD tests, each reactor was flushed with Ar to 
remove air from the headspace. Control batch tests (CTRL), without PLA 
addition, were performed under the same operating conditions to 
distinguish the contribution of PLA biodegradation from endogenous 
sludge production. Each test was carried out in triplicate.
2.3.2. Anaerobic digestion with Fenton pretreatment
A ferrous solution was prepared by dissolving 388.8 mg FeSO4⋅7H2O 
in 200 mL aqueous solution adjusted at pH = 3 with HCl (35%v/v). Af­
terwards, 0.65 g UnP-PLA or P-PLA were added to a beaker with 12.9 mL 
of ferrous solution. Then, 8 doses of 30 μL of H2O2 were added to each 
beaker every 5 min, and after 40 min, the pH was neutralized by adding 
NaOH. Finally, the soluble COD of the solution was measured, and the 
pretreated PLA sticks, namely UnP-PLA (F) and P-PLA (F), were washed, 
dried, weighed, and characterized.
A second set of PLA sticks, namely UnP-PLA (F + AD) and P-PLA (F +
AD), also underwent the above-described Fenton pretreatment and were 
subsequently used in AD tests. For these tests, both the pretreated PLA 
sticks and the respective neutralized Fenton solutions were poured into 
0.25 L PYREX glass bottles containing 0.15 L of inoculum and placed 
under mesophilic conditions (35 ± 2 ◦C) for 63 d. The reactors were 
hermetically sealed and equipped with a gas sampling port. Prior to 
incubation, the headspace was flushed with argon gas to ensure anaer­
obic conditions. Simultaneously, a blank test (CTRL) was also prepared 
without the addition of PLA. The tests were carried out in triplicate.
2.3.3. Anaerobic digestion with thermo-alkaline pretreatment
In this case, 0.65 g PLA samples were first pretreated with 13 mL 
alkaline solution (2.5 %w/v of Ca(OH)2) at different temperatures (35 ◦C 
and 70 ◦C) and durations (24 h, 48 h, and 72 h). After the pretreatment, 
the pH was neutralized with HCl (35%v/v) while the PLA sticks were 
dried and weighed, and the COD of the remaining solution was 
measured. Once the operating conditions providing the highest weight 
loss and solubilization of PLA samples were identified, the Ca(OH)2 
thermo-alkaline pretreatment was repeated on other UnP-PLA filaments 
and P-PLA sticks (samples labeled as UnP-PLA (AT) and P-PLA (AT), 
respectively). A part of these samples was collected for further proper­
ties characterization, while the remaining amount was used in AD 
treatments. In this latter case, the samples collected at the end of AD 
were labeled as UnP-PLA (AT + AD) and P-PLA (AT + AD). The bio­
logical reactors were set up as previously described for the Fenton- 
pretreated samples, and all experiments were carried out in triplicate.
2.4. Analytical methods
The content of TS and VS in the inoculum was measured by thermal 
processes, respectively at 105 ◦C and 550 ◦C, in agreement with APHA 
standard methods 2540-B and 2540-E [36].
All the liquid samples were centrifuged and filtered before the 
chemical analyses. The soluble COD of the samples was measured with 
the APHA standard method 5220-D [36] through an ONDA UV-30 SCAN 
UV-Visible spectrophotometer at 420 nm. The N-NH4
+ concentration was 
measured using an ion chromatograph (Eco IC, Metrohm) equipped with 
a Metrosep C 4 - 250/4.0 column. The concentration of P-PO4
3- was 
estimated through an Easychem Plus nutrient analyzer (Systea) 
following the US EPA method number 365.1.
The biogas volumes produced during the AD were periodically 
measured with an eudiometer and sampled to determine their compo­
sition in terms of CH4 and CO2. To this purpose, a gas chromatograph 
(8890 GC System, Agilent), equipped with a micro-packed column GC 
ShinCarbon ST, 80/100, 2 m, ID 0.53 mm (Restek) and a TCD detector, 
was used with Ar as gas carrier.
After pretreatments and digestion tests, PLA samples were washed

weight of the dried samples (Wdry) was measured. The weight loss of the

All the FT-IR data were normalized for a straightforward comparison 
and semi-quantitative analysis. Transmission data were converted to

anchors to remove slow background without distorting vibrational en­
velopes. This procedure is reported to be a useful and robust approach 
for baseline correction of vibrational spectra, which provides a stable

across the samples. The ~1454 cm−1 feature in PLA is dominated by

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Characterization of pristine PLA samples
Both UnP-PLA and P-PLA have been firstly characterized by means of 
DSC and viscometry, as reported in Table 4 and Table 5, respectively. 
DSC thermogram of pristine UnP-PLA (Fig. 2) in the first scan showed (i) 
a glass transition temperature at 66.4 ◦C immediately followed by an 
intense endothermic peak at 68 ◦C, due to the physical ageing; (ii) a 
crystallization peak in the range 90-135 ◦C (maximum at 117 ◦C); and 
(iii) a melting peak in the range of 135-170 ◦C (minimum at 153 ◦C). 
During the subsequent cooling, no crystallization phenomena were 
shown but only a Tg at 57.4 ◦C (Table S1 of the Supplementary infor­
mation). Then, the second heating scan was typical of amorphous PLA, 
with Tg at 62 ◦C, crystallization peak at 119.0 ◦C (crystallization 
enthalpy of 22.6 J/g) and sharp melting peak at 152 ◦C (melting 
enthalpy of 23.7 J/g). The melting temperature of UnP-PLA was lower 
than that of enantiomerically pure poly-L-lactic acid (170-180 ◦C), 
indicating that about 5% of the pristine PLA was present in the D-form 
[49].

Otherwise, the molecular weight of PLA after 3D printing decreased

This can be attributed to thermo-mechanical chain-scission taking place

P-PLA morphology resulting in ≈23% increase of the specific surface.
Although optical microscopy revealed a modest increase in specific 
surface area after printing, this morphological contribution was likely 
secondary to the reduction in molecular weight during PLA depoly­
merization and solubilization [50,51].
3.2. Effect of AD on PLA samples
Selected DSC thermograms of AD-treated PLAs are shown in Fig. 3, 
with evidence of glass transition temperature (Tg), crystallization peak 
(Tc) and melting peak (Tm) in the first heating scan. PLA after AD 
maintained an almost amorphous structure, as documented by the 
values of Xc reported in Table 4 (XC
1st for UnP-PLA slightly increased to 
3.2% while for P-PLA remained at 0.5%), similar to those of the pristine 
PLA.
Although thermal analyses do not directly quantify AD efficiency, 
changes in thermal transitions and degradation behavior can provide 
indirect evidence of structural modifications, depolymerization phe­
nomena, and altered hydrolytic susceptibility occurring during the 
biological process [52]. The second-run values were likewise small 
(UnP-PLA 0.7%, P-PLA 0.8%). A significant decrease of crystallization 
temperature in the first scan was also observed, from about 117 ◦C for 
pristine PLAs to about 107 ◦C, suggesting a reduction of molecular 
weight [49]. Similar behavior, even though to a lesser extent, was 
retrieved during the second scan (Table S1 of the Supplementary in­
formation). Only a slight decrease of crystallization peak from about 119

3.3. Effect of micro-aeration during AD of PLA samples
The introduction of a small amount of oxygen during AD (μAIR-AD) 
has been shown to be an effective approach to enhance the typical low 
hydrolysis rate of LMs or slow-biodegradable substrates [34,61,62]. 
Since no significant results were obtained during the AD of PLA, 
micro-aeration (μAIR) was tested with the aim of improving the sub­
strate hydrolysis rate and its subsequent biodegradation. However, both 
UnP-PLA and P-PLA did not show a significant weight loss at the end of 
an AD process lasting 60 d and carried out with the addition of 19 mL/d 
of air. On the contrary, the μAIR-AD led to an increase of the average 
biogas production of 48% compared to the conventional AD (Fig. 5). In 
fact, an average amount of 109.7 mLbiogas/gVSinoculum and 74 mLbio­
gas/gVSinoculum were obtained at the end of the AD experiments carried 
out with or without μAIR, respectively. As reported in Fig. 5a, the in­
crease in biogas production due to the μAIR can be ascribed to the 
improved bioconversion of the VS contained in the inoculum, rather 
than to the presence of the PLA. In fact, compared to the CTRL, no sig­
nificant changes in biogas production were observed in the presence of 
P-PLA, and only a slight increase of the biogas production was observed 
with UnP-PLA filaments (Fig. 5a). Accounting for the AD experiments 
carried out in the presence of UnP-PLA, the analysis of the biogas 
highlighted a significant increase of the cumulative CO2 production 
(Fig. 5b). Although μAIR-AD did not cause significant biodegradation of 
the polymer, it would appear to have had some effect on the chemical 
features of the surface of the UnP-PLA filaments. To validate this hy­
pothesis, IR analysis of the PLA samples after μAIR-AD was carried out.
The IR spectra for UnP-PLA and P-PLA after μAIR-AD (Fig. S3 of the 
Supplementary information) showed profiles that were largely super­
imposable. No variation could be observed at the ν(C=O) band, which 
remained unaltered, with similar intensity and centered at ~1747 cm−1. 
The mixed C-O-C/C-C-O/CH3-coupled region at ~1210-1040 cm−1 and 
the crystalline sensitive region (980-900 cm−1) maintained almost the 
same area ratio (IR-Cindex remained within experimental error, for 3D- 
printed samples: anaerobic 4.2, micro-aerated 4.4; for unprinted: 
anaerobic 6.8, micro-aerated 6.4, see Table S2 of the Supplementary 
information). In addition, thermograms of PLA subjected to μAIR-AD 
(not shown) were almost analogous to those of PLA after a conventional 
AD, either P-PLA or UnP-PLA, with slightly lower crystallization and 
melting temperature than pristine PLA, as documented by data reported 
in Table 4.
Consequently, the higher CO2 production observed during μAIR-AD 
was therefore best ascribed to process-level effects (oxygen-stimulated 
hydrolytic/acidogenic activity, re-oxidation of reduced inhibitors, and a 
more stable redox environment) rather than to any additional conver­
sion of PLA. This is consistent with findings in the literature [63–65], 
where it was shown that μAIR enhances hydrolysis and acidogenesis, 
suppresses accumulation of inhibitory reduced species, and stabilizes 
oxidation-reduction potential in AD systems. Additionally, the limited 
oxygen dissolution, as facultative bacteria rapidly consumed the solu­
bilized O2, likely contributed to microbial aggregate buildup, as well as 
the tolerance of some methanogens to oxygen-inhibiting effects, thereby 
improving biogas generation [63].
The limited beneficial effect of micro-aeration can be attributed to 
the intrinsic structural properties of PLA and its low susceptibility to 
oxidative and enzymatic attack under anaerobic conditions. Indeed, 
micro-aeration was successfully applied to enhance AD of other recal­
citrant substrates, such as LM. Facultative hydrolytic microorganisms, 
extracellular enzyme production, electron-transfer processes, and humic 
substance formation were probably less adequate for synthetic hydro­
phobic polyesters such as PLA [35]. Indeed, LMs contain naturally 
biodegradable polysaccharides that can be accessed by microorganisms 
under improved conditions, whereas PLA degradation remains strongly 
limited by slow ester bond hydrolysis and limited microbial accessibility 
[66]. Also, the applied air dosage of approximately 120 mL air/g VS led 
to oxygen dosages comparable to 0.38 mL O2/g VS/day reported as 
effective for LM [35]. Therefore, the limited PLA conversion obtained in 
this work cannot be ascribed to an insufficient oxygen supply during 
micro-aeration operation. Further oxygen supply could have instead 
been negative on biogas production, as reported by Zhu et al., when 
exceeding 1.6 mL/g VS/day [18], which is not the case since biogas 
yield per g SV in the control was 0.5 times higher compared to control 
without micro-aeration strategy.

3.6. Kinetic interpretation of methane production
To further investigate the effects of the different process-based 
strategies on methanation dynamics and microbial adaptation phe­
nomena, the cumulative methane yield profiles were fitted using the 
modified Gompertz equation (Eq. (6)), which is widely applied for AD 
kinetics [83]: 
G(t) = a⋅exp [ −exp( −k(t −xc))]
(6) 
where “G(t)" is the cumulative methane production at time “t" (day), “a" 
represents the ultimate methane potential (mL), “k" is the methane 
production rate (1/day), and “xc” is the acclimation time (days).
The results (Table 7) suggested that in all the investigated conditions, 
the modified Gompertz model is suitable for describing AD dynamics 
due to the high adjusted R2 values (i.e., 0.975-0.996).
In untreated samples, only limited kinetic differences were observed 
among the CTRL, UnP-PLA, and P-PLA conditions. In particular, P-PLA 
showed a slightly higher methane potential (i.e., a = 73.75 mL) and 
kinetic constant (i.e., k = 0.106 1/day) than UnP-PLA and CTRL, 
together with a slightly lower lag-phase value (i.e., xc = 7.20 days). Also, 
the modified Gompertz modeling confirmed the limited effectiveness of 
micro-aeration for PLA biodegradation. Indeed, the kinetic constant 
remained almost unchanged (i.e., k = 0.105-0.118 1/day). Similarly, the 
Fenton pretreatment did not significantly affect methane production 
kinetics, as comparable “a", “k", and “xc” values were obtained for CTRL, 
UnP-PLA, and P-PLA samples (Table 7). On the contrary, thermo- 
alkaline pretreatment significantly affected methane production ki­
netics. In particular, the highest methane-production potential was 
achieved with P-PLA (i.e., a = 265.70 mL), whereas the kinetic constant 
was improved from 0.095 to 0.209 1/day in CTRL and P-PLA, respec­
tively (Table 7).
Therefore, methane production kinetics increased by more than 2- 
fold after thermo-alkaline pretreatment (Table 7). The kinetically rele­
vant stages for AD are hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and 
methanogenesis, which are coupled with specific, functionally special­
ized microbial strains [84]. Hydrolytic and fermentative bacteria (e.g., 
Clostridium, Bacteroides, Ruminococcus, Fibrobacter, Lactobacillus, and 
Enterobacter) probably dominated hydrolysis and acidogenesis [85]. 
Accordingly, the improved methane-production kinetics (Table 7) likely 
resulted from enhanced hydrolysis and increased microbial accessibility 
to the PLA matrix (Fig. 10). Afterwards, syntrophic acetogenic bacteria 
(e.g., Syntrophomonas and Syntrophobacter) were likely to associate 
acetogenesis with H2 removal, and methanogenic archaea (e.g., Meth­
anosaeta and Methanosarcina) can subsequently conduct the final con­
version of reaction metabolites to biogas [85]. The lower “xc” values 
obtained for thermo-alkaline-treated PLA samples (Table 7) suggested a

3.7. Potential industrial application, limitations, and challenges
A preliminary energy balance was performed to support the potential 
industrial application of this approach by estimating whether the energy 
theoretically available from methane produced during AD can account 
for the energy required by the process-based strategy employed here (i. 
e., thermo-alkaline pretreatment).
The thermal energy required to heat the alkaline pretreatment me­
dium from room temperature to 70 ◦C was calculated through Eq. (7) 
[86]: 
Q = m⋅cp⋅ΔT
(7) 
where (Q) is the thermal energy required, (m) is the mass of the liquid 
phase (i.e., 13 g) or PLA (i.e., 0.65 g), (cp) is the specific heat capacity of 
the water (i.e., 4.18 kJ/kg ◦C) or the PLA (i.e., 1.8 kJ/kg ◦C [87]), and 
(ΔT) represents the increase of temperature from 25 to 70 ◦C.
Therefore, the total theoretical heating demand was 2.5 kJ. Taking 
into account the biomethane produced from P-PLA after thermo-alkaline 
pretreatment and by subtracting the contribution of the control test 
during AD (i.e., approximately 271.77 and 36.66 mL, respectively), the 
net energy recoverable from P-PLA was estimated, assuming a CH4 
lower heating value (LHV) of 35.8 MJ/m3 [88], as 8.42 kJ (ECH,4).
Finally, a positive net energy (Enet) of 5.92 kJ is obtained by sub­
tracting the energy needed for the process-based strategy (Q) from ECH,4. 
This preliminary calculation suggests that methane produced from 
thermo-alkaline-pretreated P-PLA could offset the energy required for 
the pretreatment.
Thermo-alkaline strategies were previously associated with a posi­
tive energy balance during AD processes of other substrates. For 
instance, Kim et al. [22] reported that thermo-alkaline hydrolysis 
allowed for an energy gain of 161.4 ± 39.3 MJ/ton. Similarly, 
Budych-Gorzna et al. [89] reported an improvement of methane yield 
from 210.4 to 267.1 mL CH4/gVS after low-temperature thermo-alkaline 
pretreatment of waste activated sludge, along with enhanced electricity 
recovery.
However, this calculation was intended only as a preliminary esti­
mation and did not include heat losses, mixing energy, neutralization 
requirements, reactor thermal inertia, or scale-up effects [90]. On the 
other hand, at a larger scale, the Enet could be improved by heat recovery 
(i.e., 85%) or combined heat and power (CHP) systems using the pro­
duced biogas [91,92]. Assuming a CHP electrical conversion efficiency 
of 50% and an electricity value of 86 €/MWh [89], the Enet achieved with 
the further biomethane generated after thermo-alkaline pretreatment, 
equivalent to an estimated electrical value of about 1.8 kWh/kgPLA, 
could theoretically correspond to a revenue of approximately 0.16 
€/kgPLA.
Therefore, these preliminary results indicate that a thermo-alkaline 
pretreatment here employed as a process-based strategy may have 
potential engineering feasibility if properly optimized and integrated 
into existing AD systems. However, some limitations may arise because, 
in the BMP test, important operating parameters, such as the organic 
loading rate (OLR) and hydraulic retention time (HRT), are unavailable 
in a batch system [93]. Indeed, depending on OLR, HRT, digester type, 
and other factors, the biogas produced in continuous approaches can 
differ from that produced in BMP systems. Besides volatile fatty acid 
accumulation, the washout effect and biomass accumulation, which 
affect the process stability of the AD, are not considered here. Therefore, 
further investigations under continuous or semi-continuous operating 
conditions are necessary to better evaluate the industrial applicability 
and operational feasibility of the proposed thermo-alkaline strategy.
From an environmental perspective, the global warming potential of 
AD depends on the energy vector used. In the case of biogas, after CO2 
removal using appropriate activated carbon filters [94], biomethane 
transportation can be coupled with a lower carbon footprint than heat or 
electricity production [95]. This is most likely because heat and elec­
tricity are considered lower-energy vectors, whereas the transportation 
sector relies more on fossil fuels [96].
Also, the thermo-alkaline process-based strategy requires chemical 
inputs and elevated temperatures, which can lead to an increase in 
operating complexity and parasitic energy demand [85], particularly at 
the laboratory scale, thereby increasing the environmental burden due 
to alkaline streams. In this sense, policy support can play a key role in 
making AD technologies more environmentally feasible with proper 
incentives. For instance, future investigations should also focus on 
enzymatic approaches as sustainable alternatives for improving the 
anaerobic conversion of 3D-printing-derived PLA.
4. Conclusions
This work investigated the effectiveness of different approaches for 
3D-printing-derived waste biodegradability enhancement during the AD 
process. The aim of this study was to provide a feasible solution for the 
management of polymeric residuals, which are nowadays produced in 
significant amounts after the application of widely used 3D printing 
procedures. Among the different potential wastes, attention was focused 
on PLA as one of the main materials involved in 3D printing. Accounting 
for the effect of the 3D printing, although results showed a breakage of 
the printed polymer chains resulting in a 30% decrease of its average 
molecular weight, no remarkable differences were observed during AD 
of P-PLA compared to the UnP-PLA filaments. This further highlighted 
the significance of an investigation into proper process-based strategy of 
these wastes that, despite their physical-chemical alteration after a 3D 
printing phase, can still display recalcitrant features during biological 
conversion processes. According to the outcomes from this study, similar 
results after AD with μAIR or AD following a Fenton oxidation were

on P-PLA sticks, since a 52.1% weight loss and a 39.1% solubilization 
were obtained. Also, for these tests, FT-IR spectra, DSC analysis, and 
viscometry measurements highlighted remarkable structural modifica­
tions such as an increase in crystallinity and a decrease in the average 
molecular weight (>70%). This resulted in a further weight loss during 
the following AD treatment and in a biomethane production of 319 mL/ 
gPLA and 360 mL/gPLA for UnP-PLA filaments and P-PLA sticks, respec­
tively. In particular, after 63 d of AD on the AT pretreated UnP-PLA 
filaments and P-PLA sticks an overall weight loss of 66.3% and 83.1% 
were obtained, respectively. Based on the overall outcomes, this work 
outlined different levels of effectiveness displayed by the investigated 
treatment strategies for the enhancement of 3D-printing-derived waste 
bioconversion. However, the AD performance positive results, especially 
observed on the AT pretreated PLA, still suggest the viability of the 
biological process as a strategy for the valorization of this waste cate­
gory. To strengthen the suitability of this approach, future works should 
focus on optimizing the 3D-printing process, evaluating how controlled 
modifications of the printing parameters could further enhance the 
effectiveness of pretreatments and improve the subsequent biodegra­
dation of the polymeric waste. Besides this, the optimization of oper­
ating conditions is also fundamental for the potential valorization of 
different strategies. For this aim, the assessment of the process-based 
strategy effects on the polymeric waste is crucial. This indeed high­
lights, as also observed from the results of the present work, that an 
experimental approach integrated with material characterization ana­
lyses is of significant importance to carry out more comprehensive 
studies in this research field.
